# Story 96 — SERVICE-LEVELS-3-API: record a missed deadline once and show it on the queue (Story: CRM-110)

- Story that established the sweep shape: **TICKETS-14-API (CRM-96)** — `POST /tickets/sweep-auto-close`, admin-only, one transaction per row, null audit actor, `{ closed, at }` report. Copy that shape, do not invent a second one.

## The engine, and the review before building

**SQLite, through `node:sqlite`'s `DatabaseSync`.** Every stamp in
`sla_breaches` is TEXT holding ISO-8601, and `UNIQUE (ticket_id, kind)` is
already on the table from `0003__service_levels.sql:34` — no migration is
needed for this story, and `INSERT OR IGNORE` is how a second sweep becomes
silent rather than an error. (`verify-plan` failed this plan by name for
describing persistence without saying which engine — L-5, the check that exists
because a plan once arrived written for Postgres.)

**The column is `breached_at`, not `missed_at`.** The plan names a column that
does not exist. `0003__service_levels.sql:28`.

**Both tables were already waiting.** `sla_breaches` and `escalations` exist
with exactly the unique constraints the criteria demand, written when the
schema was laid out. Neither this story nor `SERVICE-LEVELS-4-API` needs a
migration; the plan should have said so and did not check.

## Story Goal

Record a missed deadline as a stored fact (rule **S-5**): when a clock's deadline has passed and it has not stopped, write one row to `sla_breaches` (ticket id, kind, `missed_at`), enforced **once** by a unique constraint on `(ticket_id, kind)` — never by a `SELECT` running first. Reads (single-ticket and queue) surface breaches from the stored row and never recompute.

Two supporting facts land in this story:

1. Stop the **resolution** clock when a ticket is resolved (currently only `first_response` is stopped, in `conversation.service.js:142`). Without this, a sweep would record a breach against every resolved-on-time ticket.
2. Expose the breach on `publicShape` in `tickets.service.js:67` so the queue row carries it. The screen is `SERVICE-LEVELS-3-WEB (CRM-111)` — out of scope here, but the API must return the fact.

**Not in scope:** raising priority or notifying anybody (`SERVICE-LEVELS-4-API`, CRM-113); un-recording a breach; a scheduler/worker; the web screen.

## Product rules (from story)

- **Current behaviour:** breaches do not exist as rows. `readDeadlines` returns `overdue: true|false` computed on every read. Resolution clocks are never stopped.
- **New behaviour:** a stored `sla_breaches` row is the fact. `overdue` on a stored breach is a row that exists; reads never recompute the boolean when a breach row is present. Resolution clocks stop on `pending → resolved` and any other terminal status.

### 2 — Stop the resolution clock on ticket resolve

**File:** `api/src/features/tickets/tickets.service.js`

Inside the `changeStatus` method, in the branch that transitions a ticket to `resolved` (grep the file for the status literal and the transaction block), add — **inside the same transaction** and **after** the ticket row update — a call:

```js
serviceLevels.stopClock({ ticketId: id, kind: 'resolution', at });
```

Ordering follows the same rule as `pending → open`'s `resumeClock` in Story CRM-109: the SLA mutation runs after the status write so the transaction rolls back atomically. If the ticket is already `resolved` (no-op transition), do not call `stopClock`. `stopClock` returns `false` when the row is already stopped — that is fine and is not an error.

Repeat for any other terminal status the service treats as "the desk answered" (e.g. `closed` reached without going through `resolved`). Read the status graph in the service before deciding; if only `resolved` is terminal for SLA purposes, comment why.

**Pin the behaviour** in `api/src/features/tickets/status.test.js` (or the ticket-resolution test file that already exists in `api/src/features/tickets/`): after `pending → resolved`, `sla.readDeadlines({ ticketId }).resolution.stoppedAt` is set. ### 3 — Add `recordBreach` to the repository (inside-transaction helper)

**File:** `api/src/features/service-levels/service-levels.repository.js`

Add:

```js
export function recordBreach(db, { ticketId, kind, at }) {
  const stmt = db.prepare(
    `INSERT INTO sla_breaches (id, ticket_id, kind, missed_at)
     VALUES (@id, @ticketId, @kind, @at)
     ON CONFLICT (ticket_id, kind) DO NOTHING`,
  );
  const info = stmt.run({ id: generateId(), ticketId, kind, at });
  return info.changes === 1;
}
```

- Use whatever id helper the file already uses in `insertClock` (do not invent a new one).
- Return `true` if a row was written, `false` if the conflict short-circuited. The caller decides what to log; the sweep counts only rows returned `true`.
- Do **not** open a transaction inside this helper. It runs from inside the caller's transaction, exactly like `stopClock` at L102.

Also add a read helper:

```js
export function findBreachByTicket(db, { ticketId, kind }) {
  return db.prepare(
    `SELECT ticket_id AS ticketId, kind, missed_at AS missedAt
     FROM sla_breaches
     WHERE ticket_id = ? AND kind = ?`,
  ).get(ticketId, kind) ?? null;
}
```

And a bulk read used by `publicShape` (see task 6):

```js
export function findBreachesByTickets(db, { ticketIds }) {
  if (!ticketIds.length) return [];
  const placeholders = ticketIds.map(() => '?').join(',');
  return db.prepare(
    `SELECT ticket_id AS ticketId, kind, missed_at AS missedAt
     FROM sla_breaches WHERE ticket_id IN (${placeholders})`,
  ).all(...ticketIds);
}
```

### 4 — Expose `recordBreach` and `sweepBreaches` on the service

**File:** `api/src/features/service-levels/service-levels.service.js`

Import the new repository helpers next to the existing `stopClock as stopClockRow` import (L10). Extend the service factory:

- Add a comment identical in tone to L59 (`// From inside the caller's transaction, like stopClock beside it:`) explaining `recordBreach` opens no transaction.
- `recordBreach({ ticketId, kind, at })` — thin wrapper returning the repo's boolean.
- `sweepBreaches()` — the top-level entry point that:
  1. Selects candidate clocks — rows in `sla_clocks` where `stopped_at IS NULL`, that do **not** already have a matching row in `sla_breaches` (LEFT JOIN, filter NULL). Push the join into SQL; do not fetch all clocks and filter in JS. The `NOT EXISTS`/left-join makes the sweep idempotent even before the unique constraint fires.
  2. For each candidate, in **its own transaction** (mirror `sweepAutoClose` at `tickets.service.js:698`):
     - Recompute the deadline **using the same formula the read path uses** (`started_at + target_ms + paused_ms`, less `pause_started_at`-adjusted paused time if the clock is currently paused — reuse whatever `readDeadlines` calls, do not fork the maths).
     - If `now >= deadline`, call `recordBreach`. If not, do nothing.
  3. Returns `{ recorded, at }` where `recorded` is a count and `at` is the sweep timestamp. Match `sweepAutoClose`'s `{ closed, at }` return shape exactly for consistency.
  4. **Keeps going on per-row failure** — same principle as `sweepAutoClose` (L695–L697 comment). One bad row does not fail the whole sweep.
  5. Writes a null-actor audit event per recorded breach (same pattern as auto-close, so `audit.guarantee.test.js` accepts it).

Do not check "does the breach already exist" before the insert — the `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` in `recordBreach` plus the unique constraint are the only guard. The `NOT EXISTS` in step 1 is an optimisation, not a correctness gate.

## Edge Cases & Failure Modes

- **Sweep finds nothing** — writes nothing, returns `{ recorded: 0, at }`. Not an error. Enforced by the loop being a no-op when no candidates match; assert in the test plan.
- **Same clock swept twice concurrently** — two workers race between `NOT EXISTS` and `INSERT`. The unique constraint on `(ticket_id, kind)` in `sla_breaches` wins; the second `INSERT` hits `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and returns `changes === 0`. The sweep counts it as not recorded. Enforced by the schema (task 1) and `ON CONFLICT` clause (task 3).
- **Clock stopped exactly at the deadline** — no breach (the intake criterion says "a clock that stopped before its deadline records nothing" — treat `stopped_at <= deadline` as "stopped in time"). Encode the comparison as `now >= deadline AND stopped_at IS NULL` in the candidate select.
- **Paused clock whose deadline would be past if unpaused** — paused time counts (rule **S-4**). Reuse the read-path formula so paused time is not double-subtracted. Regressed via `paused-time.test.js`-style fixture.
- **Ticket resolved during the sweep** — because each row runs in its own transaction and the resolution `stopClock` (task 2) runs in the resolve transaction, either the resolve wins (clock stopped, sweep skips) or the sweep wins (breach recorded, resolve leaves it alone). Un-recording a breach is out of scope: **a missed deadline stays missed** even if the ticket resolves afterwards.
- **Sweep partial failure on row N** — the per-row transaction rolls that row back and the loop continues. Match `sweepAutoClose`'s exact log/error shape.
- **Migration on a database with orphaned unfinished clocks** — the new sweep, run for the first time, could record breaches for old clocks that were never stopped due to the pre-fix bug (task 2). See **Migration / Rollback**.
- **Clock with no matching target row** — treat as no deadline; skip. Guard with a `NOT NULL` check on the joined target row.

## Migration / Rollback

- **Migration:** if `sla_breaches` already has the `UNIQUE (ticket_id, kind)` constraint per 0003, no schema migration is required. If not, add `0016__sla_breaches_unique.sql` with `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`.
- **Backfill risk:** the first run of `sweep-breaches` in production may record breaches for old, never-stopped clocks (from the pre-fix bug where resolution clocks were not stopped on resolve). This is the desired behaviour once task 2 lands, because resolved tickets' clocks are now stopped and only genuinely-unstopped clocks remain candidates. Before running the first sweep in prod, **run a one-shot script** that back-stops resolution clocks for every already-resolved ticket using the ticket's `resolved_at`. Document the script inline in the PR description; do not check it in as a migration.
- **Rollback:** the sweep route is idempotent and additive. Revert order: (a) unregister the route, (b) drop the unique index if it was newly added (0016), (c) leave `sla_breaches` rows in place — they are correct facts. Reverting task 2 (`stopClock` on resolve) is safe on its own but re-opens the "sweep records against resolved-on-time tickets" bug; do not revert task 2 without also disabling the sweep.

## Done Criteria

- [x] A passed deadline becomes a row saying which ticket, which clock, and when it was missed.
- [x] Once, by the unique constraint — asserted directly, not only through the route.
- [x] A clock that stopped in time records nothing; the two promises are separate and a test shows one breaching while the other does not.
- [x] Paused time counts, so a ticket waiting on the customer is not recorded late.
- [x] Reads take the breach from the stored row — deleting the row stops the queue saying it, which is what "read" means and "computed" would not.
- [x] The sweep is a route, as `TICKETS-14-API` established. No scheduler, timer or worker.
- [x] A sweep that finds nothing writes nothing and is not an error; the audit row carries no actor.
- [x] Named in both censuses and in `openapi.json`. `cd api && npm test` (563), `cd web && npm test` (335), six checks green.
- [x] No commit, doc or ignore-file entry mentions AI assistance.

**One deadline expression, not two.** The sweep asks "has this fallen due" and
the queue asks "when is this due", and the moment those are two expressions
they can disagree — the sweep recording a breach the screen does not show. So
`deadlineMsFor` was extracted and both call it. That also makes S-4 and S-5
agree by construction rather than by care: the paused time is inside the one
expression.

**The handed-on finding landed here and was the real work.** Nothing stopped
the resolution clock, on any path. Without it this sweep would have recorded a
breach against every ticket the desk resolved on time — the feature reporting
failure for work done correctly. `SERVICE-LEVELS-2-API` found it, wrote it into
this story's intake, and the test for it is the one worth keeping.

**A second instance of L-62, found while wiring.** `tickets.service.js` built
its own `createServiceLevels` while compose built another for the conversation
feature. Stateless, so identical today — which is exactly what L-62 says about
two objects for one thing. The service now takes it, defaulting to its old
construction, and compose passes the one everything else holds.

**Three things the plan got wrong.** It named the column `missed_at` (it is
`breached_at`), it did not notice that `sla_breaches` and `escalations` already
exist with the constraints the criteria demand, and it described persistence
without naming the engine — which `verify-plan` failed it for by name.

Six mutations run: not stopping the clock on resolve fails 1, stamping the
breach with the sweep's own time fails 1, sweeping stopped clocks fails 3,
ignoring the pause fails 1, dropping the breaches from the queue fails 1, and
attributing the breach to the caller fails 1.

**STOP HERE. Report to the user and wait for confirmation before proceeding to SERVICE-LEVELS-4-API (CRM-113).**
